blocks.p: As soon as he saw Mr. Great-heart and his friends at the mouth of his cave with their weapons, he demanded what they wanted.
“We want you,” said Great-heart. “We have come to avenge the quarrel of the many pilgrims you have killed after dragging them out of the King’s highway. So come out of your cave.”
So he armed himself and came out, and they went to battle, and fought for more than an hour, and then stood still to catch their breath.
“Why are you here on my ground?” said the giant.
“To avenge the blood of pilgrims, as I told you before.”

So they went at it again, and the giant made Great-heart give ground; but he came on again, and in the greatness of his heart he struck so stoutly at the giant’s head and sides that he made him drop his weapon out of his hand. Then he struck him and killed him, and cut off his head, and brought it away to the inn. He also took Feeble-mind the pilgrim and brought him with him to his lodgings. When they got home they showed the head to the household, and then set it up, as they had done with others before, as a terror to anyone who might try the same thing afterward.
Then they asked Mr. Feeble-mind how he had fallen into the giant’s hands.

“I am a sickly man, as you see,” said the poor man, “and because death usually knocked at my door once a day, I thought I would never be well at home; so I took up a pilgrim’s life, and have traveled here from the town of Uncertain, where I and my father were born. I am a man of no strength at all, in body or in mind; but I would, if I could, spend my life in the pilgrim’s way, though I can only crawl along it. When I came to the gate at the head of the way, the Lord of that place received me freely. He raised no objection to my weakly looks or my feeble mind, but gave me the things I needed for my journey, and told me to hope to the end. When I came to the house of the Interpreter I received much kindness there; and because the Hill Difficulty was judged too hard for me, one of his servants carried me up it. Indeed, I have found much relief from pilgrims, though none were willing to go as slowly as I am forced to go; still, as they came up with me, they told me to be of good cheer, and said it was the will of their Lord that comfort should be given to the feeble-minded [1 Thess. 5:14], and then went on at their own pace.

“When I came up to Assault Lane, this giant met me and told me to prepare for a fight; but alas, feeble as I was, I had more need of a cordial. So he came up and took me. I didn’t imagine he would kill me. And once he had me in his den, since I had not gone with him willingly, I believed I would come out alive again; for I have heard that no pilgrim taken captive by violent hands, if he keeps his heart whole toward his Master, is allowed by the laws of Providence to die by the enemy’s hand. Robbed I expected to be, and robbed I certainly am; but as you see, I have escaped with my life, for which I thank my King as the author and you as the means. I expect other blows too; but this I have resolved: to run when I can, to walk when I cannot run, and to creep when I cannot walk. As to the main thing, I thank him who loves me, I am fixed. My way lies before me, and my mind is beyond the river that has no bridge, though I am, as you see, only of a feeble mind.”
“Weren’t you acquainted some time ago with a pilgrim named Mr. Fearing?” asked old Mr. Honest.

“Acquainted with him! Yes. He came from the town of Stupidity, which lies four degrees north of the City of Destruction, and as far again from where I was born; but we knew each other well, for he was in fact my uncle, my father’s brother. He and I were much of a temper. He was a little shorter than I am, but we were much of a complexion.”
“I can see you knew him, and I’m inclined to believe you were related; for you have his pale look, a cast of the eye like his, and your speech is much the same.”
“Most who have known us both have said so; and besides, what I read in him I have for the most part found in myself.”

“Come, sir,” said good Gaius, “cheer up. You are welcome to me and to my house. Whatever you have a mind to, call for it freely; and whatever you would have my servants do for you, they will do it with a ready mind.”

“This is unexpected kindness,” said Mr. Feeble-mind, “like the sun shining out of a very dark cloud. Did Giant Slay-good intend me this favor when he stopped me and resolved to let me go no further? Did he intend that after he had rifled my pockets I should come to Gaius my host? Yet so it is.”

Now just as Mr. Feeble-mind and Gaius were talking like this, someone came running and called at the door, and said that about a mile and a half away a pilgrim named Mr. Not-right had been struck dead by a thunderbolt on the spot where he stood.

“Alas!” said Mr. Feeble-mind. “Is he killed? He overtook me some days before I got this far, and wanted to be my companion. He was with me too when Slay-good the giant took me; but he was quick on his feet and escaped. It seems, though, that he escaped to die, and I was taken to live.”

v: What seems to seek to slay a man outright
will often save him from the saddest plight.
That very providence whose face is death
will often leave the lowly with their breath.
Taken was I; he got away and fled;
yet crossed hands gave me life, and left him dead.

blocks.p: Now about this time Matthew and Mercy were married. Gaius also gave his daughter Phoebe to James, Matthew’s brother, as his wife; and after that they stayed more than ten days longer at Gaius’s house, spending their time, and the seasons, as pilgrims do.

When they were to leave, Gaius made them a feast, and they ate and drank and were merry. Now the hour came when they must be gone, and Mr. Great-heart called for the bill; but Gaius told him that at his house it was not the custom for pilgrims to pay for their entertainment. He boarded them by the year, but looked for his payment from the good Samaritan, who had promised that at his return he would faithfully repay him whatever expense he had been put to on their account. [Luke 10:34-35]

“Beloved,” said Great-heart to him, “you do faithfully whatever you do for the brethren and for strangers, who have borne witness to your love before the church; and if you bring them forward on their journey in a godly way, you shall do well.” [3 John 5-6]
Then Gaius took his leave of them all, and of his children, and particularly of Mr. Feeble-mind. He also gave him something to drink on the way.

Now as they were going out of the door, Mr. Feeble-mind made as if he meant to linger. When Mr. Great-heart noticed it, he said, “Come, Mr. Feeble-mind, do come along with us. I will be your guide, and you shall fare as the rest do.”

“Alas,” he said, “I need a suitable companion. You are all strong and healthy; but I, as you see, am weak. So I would rather come along behind, in case, with my many infirmities, I should be a burden both to myself and to you. I am, as I said, a man of a weak and feeble mind, and I will be offended and made weak by things others can bear. I shall like no laughing; I shall like no gay clothes; I shall like no unprofitable questions. Indeed, I am so weak a man that I am offended by what others are free to do. I don’t yet know all the truth; I am a very ignorant Christian. Sometimes, if I hear others rejoicing in the Lord, it troubles me, because I cannot do the same. It is with me as with a weak man among the strong, or a sick man among the healthy, or a lamp despised (‘he that is ready to slip with his feet is as a lamp despised in the thought of him that is at ease’ [Job 12:5]), so that I don’t know what to do.”

“But brother,” said Mr. Great-heart, “I have it in my commission to ‘comfort the feeble-minded’ and to ‘support the weak.’ [1 Thess. 5:14] You must come along with us. We will wait for you; we will lend you our help [Rom. 14:1]; we will deny ourselves some things, both in opinion and in practice, for your sake [1 Cor. 8]; we will not enter into doubtful disputes in front of you; we will be made all things to you, rather than leave you behind.” [1 Cor. 9:22]

All this while they were at Gaius’s door; and as they were in the heat of this discussion, Mr. Ready-to-stumble came by, with his crutches in his hand (his crutches were the promises) [Ps. 38:17]; and he too was going on pilgrimage.

“Man, how did you come here?” said Mr. Feeble-mind to him. “I was just now complaining that I had no suitable companion, and you are exactly what I wished for. Welcome, welcome, good Mr. Ready-to-stumble; I hope you and I may be some help to each other.”
“I shall be glad of your company,” said the other. “And good Mr. Feeble-mind, rather than part, now that we’ve met so happily, I’ll lend you one of my crutches.”
“No,” he said, “though I thank you for your good will, I am not inclined to limp before I am lame. Still, I think, when the occasion comes, it may help me against a dog.”
“If either I or my crutches can do you a kindness, we are both at your command, good Mr. Feeble-mind.”
So they went on: Mr. Great-heart and Mr. Honest in front, Christiana and her children next, and Mr. Feeble-mind and Mr. Ready-to-stumble, with his crutches, behind.
“Now that we are on the road, sir,” said Mr. Honest, “tell us some profitable things about those who have gone on pilgrimage before us.”

“With a good will,” said Great-heart. “I suppose you’ve heard how Christian of old met Apollyon in the Valley of Humiliation, and what hard work he had to get through the Valley of the Shadow of Death. And I think you can’t help having heard how Faithful was put to it by Madam Wanton, by Adam the First, by one Discontent, and by Shame, four of the most deceitful villains a man can meet on the road.”
“Yes, I’ve heard all this; but indeed good Faithful was hardest put to it by Shame. He was a tireless one.”
“Yes; for as the pilgrim well said, he of all men had the wrong name.”
“But tell me, sir, where was it that Christian and Faithful met Talkative? He was a notable one too.”
“He was a confident fool, yet many follow his ways.”
“He very nearly deceived Faithful.”
“Yes, but Christian quickly put him in the way of finding him out.”
So they went on until they came to the place where Evangelist had met Christian and Faithful, and foretold what would happen to them at Vanity Fair.
“Hereabouts,” said their guide, “Christian and Faithful met Evangelist, who prophesied to them of the troubles they would meet at Vanity Fair.”
“Is that so? I daresay it was a hard chapter he read them then.”

“It was; but he gave them encouragement along with it. But why do we talk of them? They were a pair of lion-like men; they had set their faces like flint. Don’t you remember how undaunted they were when they stood before the judge?”
“Well, Faithful suffered bravely.”
“So he did, and brave things came of it; for Hopeful and some others, as the story tells it, were converted by his death.”
“Well, go on, I beg you; you know these things well.”
“Of everything Christian met with after he had passed through Vanity Fair, one Mr. Self-Interest was the arch-villain.”
“Self-Interest! What was he?”

“A very sly fellow, a downright hypocrite. One who would be religious whichever way the world went, but so cunning that he made sure never to lose or suffer for it. He had a style of religion for every new occasion, and his wife was as good at it as he was. He would turn and change from opinion to opinion, and plead for doing it too. But as far as I could learn, he came to a bad end with his self-interest; nor did I ever hear that any of his children were held in any esteem by anyone who truly feared God.”
